title: Memory graph first-pass lessons
summary: Distilled lessons from implementing the first computer-wide and options-local memory graph/dreaming loop.

entries.title: End-to-end memory work requires the requested prompt artifact
entries.body: Do not stop after building memory infrastructure. When the user asks for an end-to-end prompt or runbook, create the reusable artifact, link it globally, copy it into the target repo, and verify discoverability.

entries.title: Global memory is not project authority
entries.body: The computer-wide projects-memory graph is an index and provenance layer only. Options facts remain authoritative in repo living docs, generated readbacks, code, exact evidence artifacts, gateboard state, and data/agent-control/agent_control.db.

entries.title: Dreams cannot authorize options actions
entries.body: Dream proposals and accepted dream-origin memories are context-improvement records only. They must not authorize trading, evidence mutation, broker paths, scanner policy changes, proof-bar changes, stop or sizing changes, promotion, live validation, or protected-holdout use.

entries.title: Use hashes as write guards and provenance, not decoration
entries.body: A source hash is valuable when it proves the reviewed source has not changed before capture or promotion. If a hash mismatches, fail closed, reread the source, and redraft the memory update.

entries.title: Should runtime graph rows get SQL compare-and-swap hashes
entries.body: The first pass added file-level SHA guards for session and dream inputs, but full row-level compare-and-swap versioning for graph_nodes, graph_edges, tasks, and task reports remains a possible hardening step before multi-agent concurrent writes scale further.
